scenarios.name: protect-dashboard-nextjs16-per-resource
scenarios.rationale: A meets every rubric item: proxy.ts, ClerkProvider inside body, auth.protect() in the dashboard layout and page, a 401 re-check in the route handler, and awaited auth(). B uses proxy.ts and returns a 401 in the route handler, but it puts ClerkProvider outside <html>/<body>, protects the dashboard page only through middleware with no auth.protect() in the layout or page, and relies on createRouteMatcher.

scenarios.name: org-admin-server-action-and-ui-gating
scenarios.rationale: B uses <Show> with a permission and fallback, notes that Show is cosmetic, and awaits auth() with an orgId check and has({role:'org:admin'}), while A leans on the deprecated <Protect> as an alternative and omits <Show> entirely (though A's server action and notes are otherwise solid).

scenarios.name: sync-clerk-users-webhook-postgres
scenarios.rationale: Both use verifyWebhook, return 400 on verification failure and 2xx on success, handle both events with evt.data.id as clerkId, and cover idempotent upsert by clerkId. A gives a full middleware example that keeps the route public, a unique-index note, and more thorough security guidance, including out-of-order handling. B is more concise and correctly says not to call auth.protect() and to add the route to public routes, but its coverage is thinner. B also contains a stray reference to a 'reference' answer that the user never saw, and its user.created upsert is slightly better than A's (update: {}) at overwriting stale data.
